titleStmt.author: Howard
Viskontas
Shankar

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Ensembles of human MTL neurons “jump back in time” in response to a repeated stimulus

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether a repeated stimulus makes a neural ensemble return to the state it was in BEFORE that stimulus was first seen
span.quote: There is as yet no evidence, however, that repetition of a stimulus causes recovery of prior neural ensemble states in the MTL that would be the signature of a jump back in time.

span.label: whether cognitive models of retrieved temporal context can be told apart from short-term memory models at the level of human MTL units
span.quote: There is a disconnect in the literature between cognitive theories of episodic memory and neural circuit models of the MTL. Cognitive theories focus on the experience of mental time travel, which reinstates the learning context, thereby causing the contiguity effect. Neural circuit models of the MTL have focused on forming direct inter-item associations between neurons representing different stimuli active in short-term memory

span.label: repetition of a stimulus elicited an ensemble pattern resembling the pattern present before that stimulus was first presented, confirming a direct prediction of temporal context models
span.quote: The firing pattern of the ensemble of MTL neurons showed robust temporal autocorrelation over macroscopic periods of time during performance of the memory task. The gradually-changing part of the ensemble state was causally affected by the visual stimulus being presented. Critically, repetition of a stimulus caused the ensemble to elicit a pattern of activity that resembled the pattern of activity present before the initial presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Critically, repetition of a stimulus caused the ensemble to elicit a pattern of activity that resembled the pattern of activity present before the initial presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: neural contiguity effect in episodic memory ("jump back in time")
span.quote: The contiguity effect is an extremely robust feature of episodic memory experiments ( Kahana et al., 2008 ).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: In vivo single-neuron recordings were taken from the human MTL while epilepsy patients distinguished novel from repeated images in a continuous recognition memory task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A repeated stimulus triggers pattern completion of the gradually-changing context state that was active when it was first experienced, so the recovered state resembles states both before and after the original presentation
span.quote: Suppose that when a particular stimulus is repeated, this results in pattern completion of the gradually-changing pattern that was present when it was initially experienced.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The contiguity effect is produced by a jump back in time in which the repeated item recovers the pre-presentation state of temporal context
span.quote: In these models, the contiguity effect is caused by a “jump back in time” by which a repeated stimulus recovers the state of temporal context that was available prior to its original presentation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Long-timescale temporal autocorrelation is generated by network properties or intrinsic cellular mechanisms that sustain firing after a transient input
span.quote: The long-term temporal autocorrelation could result from either network properties or intrinsic cellular properties that lead to persistent firing in response to a transient input.

span.label: intrinsic cellular or network properties could produce persistent firing after a transient input, which is what a slowly changing representation would need
span.quote: The long-term temporal autocorrelation could result from either network properties or intrinsic cellular properties that lead to persistent firing in response to a transient input. An extensive and growing body of work from slice preparations suggests that neurons in many parts of the MTL are equipped with a variety of intrinsic mechansims that enable them to show persistent firing over long time scales in the absence of synaptic input.

span.label: recurrent CA3 connectivity could complete a gradually-changing pattern from a partial cue, which would recover the earlier context
span.quote: For decades, researchers have noted that the structure of the hippocampus, in particular the recurrent structure of CA3, could be used for autoassociative pattern completion ( Marr, 1971 ; McNaughton & Morris, 1987 ; Hasselmo & Wyble, 1997 ; Norman & O’Reilly, 2003 ). The basic idea is that during encoding, recurrent synapses are enhanced between coactive neurons. When a subset of the active neurons are reactivated during retrieval, these strengthened connections enable reactivation of the remainder of the neurons that were active during encoding.

span.label: a repeated stimulus recovers a state that is a mixture of earlier inputs weighted by temporal proximity, rather than reinstating its own original input
span.quote: However, unlike short-term memory models, in retrieved temporal context models, the contiguity effect is a result of a “jump back in time.” A repeated stimulus need not cause the same input as it did when it was first presented; a repeated stimulus can recover the state of context that was available before it was initially presented. The recovered state is, in turn, a mixture of the inputs caused by earlier stimuli weighted by their temporal proximity.

span.label: The data cannot establish whether the ensemble change caused by a stimulus's first presentation was specific to that stimulus.
span.note: what this limits: what the ensemble change means: WE CANNOT DETERMINE WITH CERTAINTY FROM THESE DATA whether the change was specific to the stimulus or general
span.quote: While we did observe strong evidence that the autocorrelated ensemble activity is causally affected by the stimuli and reflects the category membership of the stimuli, we cannot determine with certainty from these data whether the change in the ensemble activity caused by the initial presentation of a stimulus had any relationship to the particular stimulus shown.

span.label: The experiment cannot bound the longest time scale over which the ensemble representation is autocorrelated.
span.note: what this limits: the upper end of the timescale: THE RESULTS FROM THIS EXPERIMENT DO NOT PLACE A STRONG CONSTRAINT ON THE UPPER LIMIT OF THE TIME-SCALE OF THE AUTOCORRELATION
span.quote: The results from this experiment, however, do not place a strong constraint on the upper limit of the time-scale of the autocorrelation of the ensemble representation.

span.label: Averaging firing rates over 3 s windows makes any faster regional differences undetectable.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison between regions: WE AVERAGED OVER 3 s INTERVALS SO THAT DIFFERENCES BETWEEN REGIONS THAT MANIFEST ON SHORTER TIME SCALES WOULD BE INVISIBLE TO US
span.quote: Note, however, that we averaged over 3 s intervals so that differences between regions that manifest on shorter time scales would be invisible to us.

span.label: The blocked design leaves some variables (position in block, distribution of recencies, new/old ordering) uncontrolled.
span.note: what this limits: every contrast in the blocked design: IT WOULD BE IMPOSSIBLE TO COMPLETELY CONTROL ALL POSSIBLE RELEVANT VARIABLES, so position in block, recency distribution and new/old ordering ride along
span.quote: It would be impossible to completely control all possible relevant variables.

span.label: The analyses do not discriminate among mathematical forms of the gradual change.
span.note: what this limits: the functional form of the change: OUR DATA ANALYSES ASSUME THAT THE ENSEMBLE CHANGES OVER TIME BUT THEY DO NOT UNIQUELY SUPPORT A PARTICULAR MATHEMATICAL FORM OF THE CHANGE
span.quote: Although our data analyses assume that the ensemble changes over time they do not uniquely support a particular mathematical form of the change.

span.label: Recency and contiguity had to be disentangled statistically rather than by design.
span.note: what this limits: the recency-versus-contiguity separation, done statistically rather than by design: FUTURE RESEARCH SHOULD DISENTANGLE RECENCY FROM CONTIGUITY BY, FOR INSTANCE, PRESENTING REPEATED STIMULI AFTER A LONG DELAY
span.quote: Future research should disentangle recency from contiguity by, for instance, presenting repeated stimuli after a long delay.

span.label: the mechanistic account of how the jump back in time is accomplished is labelled necessarily speculative
span.note: what this limits: the mechanistic account that follows: WHILE NECESSARILY SPECULATIVE, IT IS WORTH THINKING ABOUT HOW THESE TWO FUNCTIONS MIGHT BE ACCOMPLISHED
span.quote: While necessarily speculative, it is worth thinking about how these two functions might be accomplished.

span.label: the data cannot settle what exactly is retrieved when the ensemble state is recovered
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - what exactly is retrieved is undetermined
span.quote: While we did observe strong evidence that the autocorrelated ensemble activity is causally affected by the stimuli and reflects the category membership of the stimuli, we cannot determine with certainty from these data

span.label: firing was averaged over three-second intervals, so regional differences on shorter timescales could not be seen
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 2 - the 3 s averaging hides faster regional differences
span.quote: Note, however, that we averaged over 3 s intervals so that differences between regions that manifest on shorter time scales would be invisible to us.

span.label: some design variables cannot be controlled at all: the first stimulus of a block is necessarily new and the last necessarily old
span.note: what this limits: the blocked design: IT IS NECESSARILY THE CASE THAT THE FIRST STIMULUS SHOWN IN A BLOCK IS NEW AND THE LAST STIMULUS IN THE BLOCK IS OLD
span.quote: It would be impossible to completely control all possible relevant variables. For instance, it is necessarily the case that the first stimulus shown in a block is new and the last stimulus in the block is old. There is a general tendency for there to be more old stimuli later in the block than earlier in the block. In addition, the recencies that can be sampled at any one time depend on the position within the block and the stimuli that have been previously presented.

span.label: autocorrelated units did not show robust stimulus coding by this method, only category specificity
span.note: what this limits: the stimulus-coding claim: ROBUST STIMULUS CODING WAS NOT OBSERVED USING THIS METHOD IN THE TEMPORALLY-AUTOCORRELATED PART OF THE ENSEMBLE, t(15) = 0.46 - only category specificity was
span.quote: Robust stimulus coding was not observed using this method in the temporally-autocorrelated part of the ensemble, t(15) = 0.46. 2 However, there was robust category-specificity in the temporally-autocorrelated part of the ensemble; similarity was greater for comparisons between same-category event pairs than between different-category pairs

span.label: retrieved temporal context, brought from list-memory modelling to a prediction about single units
span.quote: However, unlike short-term memory models, in retrieved temporal context models, the contiguity effect is a result of a “jump back in time.” A repeated stimulus need not cause the same input as it did when it was first presented; a repeated stimulus can recover the state of context that was available before it was initially presented. The recovered state is, in turn, a mixture of the inputs caused by earlier stimuli weighted by their temporal proximity.

span.label: recency and contiguity as the two effects any account must produce
span.quote: Episodic memory exhibits two extremely robust temporal effects in the laboratory: the recency effect and the contiguity effect. The recency effect describes the finding that more recently presented items are better remembered ( Murdock, 1962 ; Glenberg et al., 1980 ), while the contiguity effect refers to the finding that when a stimulus from a list is remembered, memory for other stimuli nearby in the list is enhanced

span.label: the analysis restricted to pairs of events WITHIN THE SAME BLOCK, which were necessarily from the same category
span.quote: In order to avoid artifactual category-specific contiguity effects, we restricted our attention to pairs of events within the same block

span.label: category → event number
span.note: THE TWO CANNOT BE SEPARATED IN THIS STUDY - the DESIGN form of the negative relation (Q-286/Q-287). No edge type can express it: all eight assert that a relation HOLDS. Recorded here because a confounding statement BOUNDS WHAT THE PAPER'S OWN RESULTS CAN MEAN, and it lives in a methods paragraph where nothing downstream will find it. A design confound stated plainly in a methods sentence.
span.quote: Because of the blocked structure of this experiment, the category of the stimulus is confounded with the event number.

span.label: THE TWO RIVALS ARE MADE TO AGREE EVERYWHERE BUT ONE PLACE: both predict a gradually changing state caused by the stimuli, and the paper says so before testing anything
span.quote: If it is physically implemented, the retrieved temporal context approach requires that the state of the memory system should change gradually over time and that these changes should be caused by the stimuli presented. These predictions are shared with short-term memory models.

span.label: and the discriminating prediction is an ASYMMETRY: short-term memory predicts resemblance only to states AFTER the original presentation, a jump back in time predicts resemblance in both directions
span.quote: The unique predictions of the retrieved temporal context approach are manifest when one considers the comparison between the neural response caused by a repeated stimulus and the neighbors of its original presentation. If a gradually-changing memory state were a signature of a short-term memory that contains stimuli, then the input caused by the repeated stimulus would resemble the states of the short-term memory following its original presentation, when that stimulus was still active in short-term memory. The overlap between the repeated state should decrease going forward from the original presentation as that stimulus decays in short-term memory. However, if repeating a stimulus causes a jump back in time then the state caused by the repeated stimulus will be similar to neighboring states in both the forward and backward directions.

span.label: a jump back in time is defined as recovering the context that existed BEFORE the stimulus was first presented, not as reinstating the stimulus's own input
span.quote: However, unlike short-term memory models, in retrieved temporal context models, the contiguity effect is a result of a “jump back in time.” A repeated stimulus need not cause the same input as it did when it was first presented; a repeated stimulus can recover the state of context that was available before it was initially presented. The recovered state is, in turn, a mixture of the inputs caused by earlier stimuli weighted by their temporal proximity.

span.label: temporally-autocorrelated is an operational label: units whose lag-one regression coefficient on the previous event's firing rate is significantly above zero, about a quarter of all units
span.quote: The distribution of lag one regression coefficients across units was significantly greater than zero, mean .094 ± .01, t(269) = 9.31, p < .001 (see Figure 3a ). We refer to units that had a lag one regression coefficient significantly greater than zero (p < .05) as temporally-autocorrelated units. Almost one quarter of all units recorded (.248) were classified as temporally-autocorrelated units.

span.label: each unit is treated as an independent observation and as a one-cell ensemble, because unit counts vary across sessions and sessions were at least 48 hours apart
span.quote: Because of the variability in the number of units across recording sessions ( Table 1 ), we do not simply report means averaged across sessions. Rather, the mean values report the average across units. That is, for the purposes of doing statistics, each unit was treated as a one-cell ensemble. Because recording sessions from a particular patient were separated by at least 48 hours, we treated each unit as an independent observation.

span.label: the design was chosen over free recall precisely because repetition order is under experimenter control rather than following the subject's own retrieval
span.quote: Because the sequence of repetitions is under experimental control rather than a consequence of the subject’s own retrieval strategy it provides a better opportunity to assess the causal relationship between repetition of a stimulus and the jump back in time.

span.label: claim_type: existence
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: existence — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: These findings confirm a direct prediction of this class of temporal context models and may be a signature of the mechanism that underlies the experience of episodic memory as mental time travel.

span.label: method: microwire single-unit recording during a continuous recognition task, with ensemble similarity analysed as a function of recency and of lag from the original presentation
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: electrophysiology — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Because the sequence of repetitions is under experimental control rather than a consequence of the subject’s own retrieval strategy it provides a better opportunity to assess the causal relationship between repetition of a stimulus and the jump back in time.

span.label: phenomenon: temporal autocorrelation of MTL ensemble firing over tens of seconds, with a contiguity effect superimposed on it
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: neural contiguity effect in episodic memory ("jump back in time") — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: To anticipate the results, units will show temporal autocorrelation over tens of seconds. The contiguity analysis will both rule out the possibility that the temporal autocorrelation is solely a recording artifact and also demonstrate both forward and backward contiguity effects, confirming a key prediction of the retrieved context approach.

span.label: builds-on → retrieved temporal context models of episodic memory
span.quote: These findings confirm a direct prediction of this class of temporal context models and may be a signature of the mechanism that underlies the experience of episodic memory as mental time travel.

span.label: extends → Manning et al. (2011)
span.quote: Manning et al. (2011) used a similar strategy to analyze human ECoG during performance of a free recall task.

span.label: contradicts → Norman and O'Reilly (2003)
span.quote: Similarly, the Norman and O’Reilly (2003) model as published would not account for the neural contiguity effect but could be elaborated to do so.

span.label: contradicts → accounts identifying the MTL ensemble with persistent stimulus-specific activation in short-term memory
span.quote: Although the results of the contiguity analysis are not predicted by identification of the MTL ensemble with persistent stimulus-specific activation, our findings could be accommodated within existing mathematical cognitive models of short-term memory.

span.label: contradicts → short-term memory accounts in which contiguity comes from persistent stimulus activation and direct inter-item associations
span.quote: The backward effect in Figure 4c is not predicted by persistent stimulus activation in short-term memory but is predicted by a jump back in time.

span.label: supports → retrieved temporal context models of recency and contiguity
span.quote: These findings confirm a direct prediction of this class of temporal context models and may be a signature of the mechanism that underlies the experience of episodic memory as mental time travel.

span.label: extends → Manning 2011's finding that recall reinstates the pattern present during study of preceding items
span.note: status: the paper's own words: is not clear
span.quote: However, there are two important limitations of that study. First, it is not clear whether the context reinstatement effect generalizes to the level of units. Second, because the order of free recall is unconstrained the study leaves open the possibility that the neural state during retrieval of an item resembles the activity associated with preceding items because those preceding items were recalled shortly before the target work.

span.label: contradicts → models in which the gradually changing memory representation is independent of the stimuli presented
span.quote: Our results show strong evidence that the MTL maintains a representation that changes gradually over time that is not attributable to recording artifacts nor to uncontrolled experimental variables. These accounts would have predicted a flat curve in Figure 4c .

span.label: builds-on → evidence for temporal autocorrelation and stimulus selectivity in MTL neurons
span.quote: There is as yet no evidence, however, that repetition of a stimulus causes recovery of prior neural ensemble states in the MTL that would be the signature of a jump back in time.

span.label: temporal context —contrasted-with→ short-term memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE RIVALS AGREE ON PURPOSE: both require a state that changes gradually and is caused by the stimuli, and the paper says so BEFORE testing
span.quote: If it is physically implemented, the retrieved temporal context approach requires that the state of the memory system should change gradually over time and that these changes should be caused by the stimuli presented. These predictions are shared with short-term memory models.

span.label: jump back in time —distinct-from→ short-term memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — AND THEY DIFFER IN EXACTLY ONE PLACE: short-term memory predicts resemblance only FORWARD of the original presentation, a jump back predicts it in both directions
span.quote: The unique predictions of the retrieved temporal context approach are manifest when one considers the comparison between the neural response caused by a repeated stimulus and the neighbors of its original presentation. If a gradually-changing memory state were a signature of a short-term memory that contains stimuli, then the input caused by the repeated stimulus would resemble the states of the short-term memory following its original presentation, when that stimulus was still active in short-term memory. The overlap between the repeated state should decrease going forward from the original presentation as that stimulus decays in short-term memory. However, if repeating a stimulus causes a jump back in time then the state caused by the repeated stimulus will be similar to neighboring states in both the forward and backward directions.

span.label: jump back in time —part-of→ temporal context
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the recovered state is a mixture of earlier inputs weighted by proximity, NOT a reinstatement of the stimulus's own input
span.quote: However, unlike short-term memory models, in retrieved temporal context models, the contiguity effect is a result of a “jump back in time.” A repeated stimulus need not cause the same input as it did when it was first presented; a repeated stimulus can recover the state of context that was available before it was initially presented. The recovered state is, in turn, a mixture of the inputs caused by earlier stimuli weighted by their temporal proximity.

span.label: temporal autocorrelation —distinct-from→ artifact
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE ARTEFACT CLASS IS DEFINED BY WHAT IT CANNOT KNOW: no recording artefact can make spike shape depend on WHICH picture was shown, so stimulus-specificity excludes the whole class
span.quote: Artifactual accounts of the temporal autocorrelation require that there be no causal relationship between the stimuli being presented and the gradually-changing ensemble response. To take one example, although the shape of action potentials recorded extracellularly might change over time, leading to an artifactual temporal autocorrelation in the ensemble response, there is no reason to suspect that the specific identity of the picture presented to the patient affects the shape of the action potential.

span.label: artifact —distinct-from→ MTL
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the gradually changing representation is attributable neither to recording artefacts nor to uncontrolled experimental variables - both would have predicted a flat curve
span.quote: Our results show strong evidence that the MTL maintains a representation that changes gradually over time that is not attributable to recording artifacts nor to uncontrolled experimental variables. These accounts would have predicted a flat curve in Figure 4c .

span.label: block —causes→ category
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE DESIGN BUILDS THE CONFOUND IN: category is confounded with event number, so recent comparisons are also same-category comparisons
span.quote: Because of the blocked structure of this experiment, the category of the stimulus is confounded with the event number. As a consequence, comparisons that are recent are also likely to be stimuli from the same category. In order to isolate the effects of stimulus and category in relative isolation of recency, ensemble similarities were aggregated as a function of recency separately for a) comparisons between presentations of the same stimulus, b) pairs in which both stimuli were from the same category (faces or scenes) but were different stimuli, and c) pairs in which the stimuli were from different categories. In order to assess the effect of these variables independently of recency, we performed comparisons across pairs of similarities with the same recency.

span.label: recency —distinct-from→ category
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — SEPARATED BY MATCHING: comparisons are made across pairs of similarities at the SAME recency, so the difference cannot be recency
span.quote: Second, MTL ensembles captured information about properties of the stimuli other than stimulus identity. The ensemble similarity between same-category pairs was greater than for different-category pairs, t(56) = 13.9, p < .001. Because this comparison is across recencies, the difference cannot be attributed to a confounding of recency and category structure.

span.label: block —distinct-from→ temporal autocorrelation
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — and the block structure is removed by restricting every comparison to pairs of events inside one block
span.quote: To isolate temporal autocorrelation from the effects of stimulus category and block (which were also autocorrelated in time due to the structure of the experiment) we restricted our attention to pairs of events within the same block.

span.label: lag —distinct-from→ recency
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — THE AXIS IS SWAPPED ON PURPOSE: results are aggregated not by recency of the comparison but by distance from the ORIGINAL presentation of the repeated stimulus
span.quote: For each repeated stimulus, we compared the ensemble activity for that event to preceding events from the same block and aggregated the results, not as a function of the recency of the comparison, but as a function of the lag between the earlier event and the initial presentation of the repeated stimulus.

span.label: recency —causes→ ensemble similarity
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — and the recency gradient is then ESTIMATED and SUBTRACTED, so what remains is the contiguity effect alone
span.quote: To statistically remove the recency effect, we estimated the results of the contiguity analysis we would have obtained if recency were the only factor causing ensemble similarity.

span.label: persistent firing —causes→ temporal autocorrelation
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The long-term temporal autocorrelation could result from either network properties or intrinsic cellular properties that lead to persistent firing in response to a transient input. An extensive and growing body of work from slice preparations suggests that neurons in many parts of the MTL are equipped with a variety of intrinsic mechansims that enable them to show persistent firing over long time scales in the absence of synaptic input.

span.label: pattern completion —causes→ jump back in time
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — offered as the recovery mechanism, from the recurrent structure of CA3
span.quote: If there is a gradually-changing representation of recent experience accessible to the MTL, this naturally raises the question of how it could be recovered to implement a jump back in time. For decades, researchers have noted that the structure of the hippocampus, in particular the recurrent structure of CA3, could be used for autoassociative pattern completion

span.label: hippocampus —contrasted-with→ amygdala
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — A REGIONAL NULL: hippocampus, parahippocampal region and entorhinal cortex all far exceed the Type I error rate and do not differ from each other; the amygdala does not exceed it at all
span.quote: The proportion of temporally-autocorrelated units in the hippocampus, parahippocampal region, and entorhinal cortex far exceeded the Type I error rate (.05) and did not reliably differ among those regions, χ 2 (2) = 4.87, p > .05 (see Table 2 ). The number of units in the amygdala classified as temporally-autocorrelated did not exceed the Type I error rate.

span.label: continuous recognition —operationalised-as→ jump back in time
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — chosen over free recall BECAUSE the repetition order is set by the experimenter rather than by the subject's retrieval
span.quote: This paper reports results from single-unit recordings from the human MTL that address this gap using a continuous recognition experiment. Because the sequence of repetitions is under experimental control rather than a consequence of the subject’s own retrieval strategy it provides a better opportunity to assess the causal relationship between repetition of a stimulus and the jump back in time.

span.label: recency effect —contrasted-with→ contiguity effect
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the two behavioural effects any account must produce, and here they appear superimposed in one curve
span.quote: Episodic memory exhibits two extremely robust temporal effects in the laboratory: the recency effect and the contiguity effect. The recency effect describes the finding that more recently presented items are better remembered ( Murdock, 1962 ; Glenberg et al., 1980 ), while the contiguity effect refers to the finding that when a stimulus from a list is remembered, memory for other stimuli nearby in the list is enhanced

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: A linear regression showed a significant effect of recency on ensemble similarity, regression coefficient .006 ± .001, F (1, 17) = 53.3, p < .001.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The distribution of lag one regression coefficients across units was significantly greater than zero, mean .094 ± .01, t(269) = 9.31, p < .001 (see Figure 3a ).

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Same-stimulus pairs were more similar than same category-pairs, paired t-test across recencies, t(15) = 3.18, p < .01.

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: The proportion of temporally-autocorrelated units in the hippocampus, parahippocampal region, and entorhinal cortex far exceeded the Type I error rate (.05) and did not reliably differ among those regions, χ 2 (2) = 4.87, p > .05 (see Table 2 ).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: An ANOVA with |lag| as a regressor and direction (forward vs backward) as a categorical variable yielded a main effect of the absolute value of lag, F (1, 18) = 13.1, MSe = .0081, p < .002, definitively demonstrating that the autocorrelation in the ensemble cannot be solely caused by random variation independent of the identity of the stimuli.

span.label: z-score standardisation
span.quote: To compare ensemble similarities of event vectors, we z-transformed each unit’s activity across events prior to taking a weighted inner product.

span.label: lag one regression coefficient
span.quote: The distribution of lag one regression coefficients across units was significantly greater than zero, mean .094 ± .01, t(269) = 9.31, p < .001 (see Figure 3a ). We refer to units that had a lag one regression coefficient significantly greater than zero (p < .05) as temporally-autocorrelated units. Almost one quarter of all units recorded (.248) were classified as temporally-autocorrelated units.

span.label: Type I error rate
span.quote: The proportion of temporally-autocorrelated units in the hippocampus, parahippocampal region, and entorhinal cortex far exceeded the Type I error rate (.05) and did not reliably differ among those regions, χ 2 (2) = 4.87, p > .05 (see Table 2 ). The number of units in the amygdala classified as temporally-autocorrelated did not exceed the Type I error rate.

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Second, MTL ensembles captured information about properties of the stimuli other than stimulus identity. The ensemble similarity between same-category pairs was greater than for different-category pairs, t(56) = 13.9, p < .001. Because this comparison is across recencies, the difference cannot be attributed to a confounding of recency and category structure.

span.label: MTL ensemble activity changed gradually over tens of seconds and this drift was causally tied to which stimulus was shown, not to recording artifact.
span.quote: The ensemble response changed gradually over tens of seconds and was causally affected by the identity of the stimulus presented.

span.label: Repeating a stimulus recovered ensemble activity that had been present before its original presentation — a reliable backward contiguity effect.
span.quote: The contiguity analysis showed a statistically reliable backward effect ( Figure 4c ) confirming a prediction of models that postulate that the contiguity effect results from a jump back in time of a neural representation.

span.label: Ensemble similarity also fell off in the forward direction, which is consistent with either short-term memory or retrieved-context accounts.
span.quote: There was a significant decrease in similarity as a function of |lag| in the forward direction, .008 ± .003, F (1, 9) = 7.04, p < .03, consistent with both short-term memory and retrieved context accounts.

span.label: MTL ensembles carried category information above and beyond stimulus identity, independent of recency.
span.quote: The ensemble similarity between same-category pairs was greater than for different-category pairs, t(56) = 13.9, p < .001.

span.label: The temporally autocorrelated subset of units did not itself show robust individual-stimulus coding, although it did show category specificity.
span.quote: Robust stimulus coding was not observed using this method in the temporally-autocorrelated part of the ensemble, t(15) = 0.46.

span.label: The contiguity analysis rules out spike-sorting or environmental artifacts as the sole source of the observed temporal autocorrelation.
span.quote: Although artifacts may exist, the contiguity analysis provides very strong evidence against the hypothesis that all of the temporal autocorrelation in ensemble activity is due to artifactual sources.

span.label: THE RIVALS SHARE TWO PREDICTIONS BY CONSTRUCTION: both require a gradually changing state caused by the presented stimuli
span.quote: If it is physically implemented, the retrieved temporal context approach requires that the state of the memory system should change gradually over time and that these changes should be caused by the stimuli presented. These predictions are shared with short-term memory models.

span.label: AND DIFFER IN ONE ASYMMETRY: short-term memory predicts resemblance only to states following the original presentation, a jump back in time predicts both directions
span.quote: The unique predictions of the retrieved temporal context approach are manifest when one considers the comparison between the neural response caused by a repeated stimulus and the neighbors of its original presentation. If a gradually-changing memory state were a signature of a short-term memory that contains stimuli, then the input caused by the repeated stimulus would resemble the states of the short-term memory following its original presentation, when that stimulus was still active in short-term memory. The overlap between the repeated state should decrease going forward from the original presentation as that stimulus decays in short-term memory. However, if repeating a stimulus causes a jump back in time then the state caused by the repeated stimulus will be similar to neighboring states in both the forward and backward directions.

span.label: so the signature sought is a repeated stimulus recovering activity present BEFORE its original presentation
span.quote: That is, the signature of the jump back in time is that a repeated stimulus recovers activity that was present prior to the original presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: lag one regression coefficients were above zero overall and about a quarter of units qualified as temporally autocorrelated
span.quote: The distribution of lag one regression coefficients across units was significantly greater than zero, mean .094 ± .01, t(269) = 9.31, p < .001 (see Figure 3a ). We refer to units that had a lag one regression coefficient significantly greater than zero (p < .05) as temporally-autocorrelated units. Almost one quarter of all units recorded (.248) were classified as temporally-autocorrelated units.

span.label: autocorrelated units fired above baseline BEFORE the stimulus appeared, so they were not simply responding to it
span.quote: Autocorrelated units showed elevated firing in the time prior to stimulus presentation suggesting they were not simply responding to the just-presented stimulus.

span.label: hippocampus, parahippocampal region and entorhinal cortex all far exceeded the Type I error rate; the amygdala did not
span.quote: The proportion of temporally-autocorrelated units in the hippocampus, parahippocampal region, and entorhinal cortex far exceeded the Type I error rate (.05) and did not reliably differ among those regions, χ 2 (2) = 4.87, p > .05 (see Table 2 ). The number of units in the amygdala classified as temporally-autocorrelated did not exceed the Type I error rate.

span.label: BLOCK STRUCTURE REMOVED BY RESTRICTION: all comparisons confined to pairs of events within one block, which are necessarily same-category
span.quote: To isolate temporal autocorrelation from the effects of stimulus category and block (which were also autocorrelated in time due to the structure of the experiment) we restricted our attention to pairs of events within the same block.

span.label: A LOWER BOUND ON THE TIMESCALE: excluding the eight nearest recencies still left a significant slope, so the ensemble kept changing past 27 seconds
span.quote: The change over time was not simply due to an elevated level of ensemble similarity for adjacent events. A regression excluding recencies −8 to −1, focusing on just recencies −19 to −9, still found a significant regression coefficient, .003 ± .001, F (1, 9) = 5.64, p < .05. This analysis sets a lower limit on the time scale of the change over time. Because the similarity continued to decrease after recency −9, this means that the ensemble continued changing reliably after nine intervening stimuli, or a delay of more than 27 s.

span.label: CATEGORY AND RECENCY SEPARATED BY MATCHING: comparisons made across pairs of similarities at the same recency
span.quote: Because of the blocked structure of this experiment, the category of the stimulus is confounded with the event number. As a consequence, comparisons that are recent are also likely to be stimuli from the same category. In order to isolate the effects of stimulus and category in relative isolation of recency, ensemble similarities were aggregated as a function of recency separately for a) comparisons between presentations of the same stimulus, b) pairs in which both stimuli were from the same category (faces or scenes) but were different stimuli, and c) pairs in which the stimuli were from different categories. In order to assess the effect of these variables independently of recency, we performed comparisons across pairs of similarities with the same recency.

span.label: so the category effect cannot be attributed to the confounding of recency with category structure
span.quote: Second, MTL ensembles captured information about properties of the stimuli other than stimulus identity. The ensemble similarity between same-category pairs was greater than for different-category pairs, t(56) = 13.9, p < .001. Because this comparison is across recencies, the difference cannot be attributed to a confounding of recency and category structure.

span.label: A DISSOCIATION INSIDE THE ENSEMBLE: the autocorrelated units showed category specificity but not robust stimulus coding, t = 0.46
span.quote: Robust stimulus coding was not observed using this method in the temporally-autocorrelated part of the ensemble, t(15) = 0.46. 2 However, there was robust category-specificity in the temporally-autocorrelated part of the ensemble; similarity was greater for comparisons between same-category event pairs than between different-category pairs

span.label: while the non-autocorrelated units showed both stimulus and category selectivity
span.quote: The non-autocorrelated part of the ensemble showed robust stimulus and category selectivity. Across recencies, same-stimulus comparisons showed greater similarity than did same-category comparison, t(15) = 4.55, p < .001. Similarly, within-category comparisons were more similar to one another than between-category comparisons

span.label: THE ARTEFACT CLASS DEFINED BY WHAT IT CANNOT KNOW: no recording artefact would make spike shape depend on which picture was shown
span.quote: Artifactual accounts of the temporal autocorrelation require that there be no causal relationship between the stimuli being presented and the gradually-changing ensemble response. To take one example, although the shape of action potentials recorded extracellularly might change over time, leading to an artifactual temporal autocorrelation in the ensemble response, there is no reason to suspect that the specific identity of the picture presented to the patient affects the shape of the action potential.

span.label: ONE ANALYSIS SERVING TWO PURPOSES: the contiguity analysis both diagnoses a causal link to the stimulus and looks for the jump back in time
span.quote: The analysis allows us to diagnose a causal relationship between the stimulus presented and the gradually-changing response, ruling out artifactual accounts of the temporal autocorrelation. It also enables us to look for the neural signature of a jump back in time.

span.label: and the question is declared meaningless for units that are not autocorrelated in the first place
span.quote: It does not make sense to ask about whether the neural signature of mental time travel is observed in units that do not show temporal autocorrelation.

span.label: SORTING ERROR ONE ANSWERED: splitting one neuron across units could fake autocorrelation but not stimulus specificity, block sensitivity, or retained information about preceding stimuli
span.quote: In one type of error, a single neuron could have spikes sorted into multiple units. If whatever factors that favor one unit over the other are autocorrelated, then this type of error could result in an artifactual autocorrelation. This artifact, however, could not account for the stimulus-specificity, sensitivity of the ensemble to the block structure, or the fact that the autocorrelated signal retains information about preceding stimuli.

span.label: SORTING ERROR TWO ANSWERED: merging neurons could fake conjunctions, but not a response to the neighbours of a particular stimulus's original presentation
span.quote: In the other type of error, spikes from multiple neurons are counted as belonging to one unit. This type of error could lead to artifactual conjunctions in the properties of units. For instance, if spikes from a stimulus-specific neuron were counted as part of the same unit as an autocorrelated neuron, we might incorrectly conclude that there was an autocorrelated stimulus-specific cell. Because the identity of the stimulus affects the response to the neighbors of the original presentation of the stimulus, the results of our contiguity analysis is not subject to this type of artifact either.

span.label: curves peaked at zero and falling off both ways would otherwise require the particular picture to change the shape of recorded spikes
span.quote: The fact that the contiguity analyses resulted in curves that are peaked around zero and fall off gradually, in both the forward or the backward direction means that there is a causal relationship between the stimulus being presented to the patient and autocorrelated ensemble activity. If this result were an artifact, this would require that there is a causal relationship between the particular stimulus being shown to the patient and the shape of the spikes being recorded.

span.label: AND AN ENVIRONMENTAL CLASS RULED OUT TOO: a fan or other sound present during part of a session cannot produce a contiguity effect
span.quote: The contiguity analysis also rules out the possibility that the temporal autocorrelation results from uncontrolled environmental stimuli that are extended in time ( Mensink & Raaijmakers, 1988 ; Estes, 1955 ; Murdock, 1997 ). For instance, perhaps a cell fired for part of the recording session because there was a fan or other environmental sound that was present only during that part of the session.

span.label: the artefactual and stimulus-independent accounts would both have predicted a flat curve
span.quote: Our results show strong evidence that the MTL maintains a representation that changes gradually over time that is not attributable to recording artifacts nor to uncontrolled experimental variables. These accounts would have predicted a flat curve in Figure 4c .

span.label: THE DECIDING RESULT: the backward effect is not predicted by persistent stimulus activation but is predicted by a jump back in time
span.quote: The backward effect in Figure 4c is not predicted by persistent stimulus activation in short-term memory but is predicted by a jump back in time.

span.label: the recency gradient was estimated and subtracted so that what remained on the lag axis was contiguity alone
span.quote: To statistically remove the recency effect, we estimated the results of the contiguity analysis we would have obtained if recency were the only factor causing ensemble similarity.

span.label: SOME CONFOUNDS ARE STRUCTURAL AND UNCONTROLLABLE: the first stimulus of a block is necessarily new and the last necessarily old
span.quote: It would be impossible to completely control all possible relevant variables. For instance, it is necessarily the case that the first stimulus shown in a block is new and the last stimulus in the block is old. There is a general tendency for there to be more old stimuli later in the block than earlier in the block. In addition, the recencies that can be sampled at any one time depend on the position within the block and the stimuli that have been previously presented.

span.label: the prior free-recall result had two named limitations: it was not at unit level, and recall order was set by the subject
span.quote: However, there are two important limitations of that study. First, it is not clear whether the context reinstatement effect generalizes to the level of units. Second, because the order of free recall is unconstrained the study leaves open the possibility that the neural state during retrieval of an item resembles the activity associated with preceding items because those preceding items were recalled shortly before the target work.

span.label: which is why repetition under experimenter control gives a better test of the causal relationship
span.quote: Because the sequence of repetitions is under experimental control rather than a consequence of the subject’s own retrieval strategy it provides a better opportunity to assess the causal relationship between repetition of a stimulus and the jump back in time.

span.label: UNIT CRITERIA STATED NUMERICALLY: clear refractory periods, amplitude over 100 microvolts, under 1 percent of spikes below 3 ms
span.quote: Single units were defined as waveforms with clear refractory periods, that were of high amplitude (> 100 microvolts), and had less than 1% of spikes occurring at less than 3 ms.

span.label: with a power-spectrum check discarding units carrying significant 60 Hz line noise
span.quote: As an additional check for noise, we plotted the power spectral density using the times when spikes occurred for that unit; putative cell activity showing significant amounts of 60 Hz power-line activity was excluded from further analysis.

span.label: and every unit inspected by a human observer as well as by the clustering algorithm
span.quote: Each and every unit was observed and evaluated by a human observer in addition to the clustering algorithm.

span.label: the three-second analysis window is shorter than the minimum inter-stimulus interval, so no spike is counted twice
span.quote: The minimum amount of time between presentation of stimuli, including the time for the behavioral response, was 3.10 s, so there is no chance that a single spike is counted as part of in two separate events.

span.label: patients discriminated new from old reliably with no bias, hit rate .82 and correct rejection .83
span.quote: The patients were able to reliably discriminate new from previously-seen stimuli and showed no trend toward a bias (hit rate = .82 ± .07; correct rejection rate = .83 ± .07).

span.label: recency effect and contiguity effect
span.quote: The recency effect describes the finding that more recently presented items are better remembered ( Murdock, 1962 ; Glenberg et al., 1980 ), while the contiguity effect refers to the finding that when a stimulus from a list is remembered, memory for other stimuli nearby in the list is enhanced ( Kahana, 1996 ; Kahana, Howard, & Polyn, 2008 ).

span.label: temporally-autocorrelated units
span.quote: We refer to units that had a lag one regression coefficient significantly greater than zero (p < .05) as temporally-autocorrelated units.

span.label: jump back in time (neural signature of)
span.term: jump back in time (neural signature of)
span.quote: That is, the signature of the jump back in time is that a repeated stimulus recovers activity that was present prior to the original presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: lag one regression coefficient
span.quote: We refer to the fitted value of φ as the lag one regression coefficient (see e.g., Figure 3a ).

span.label: contiguity effect
span.quote: Episodic memory exhibits two extremely robust temporal effects in the laboratory: the recency effect and the contiguity effect. The recency effect describes the finding that more recently presented items are better remembered ( Murdock, 1962 ; Glenberg et al., 1980 ), while the contiguity effect refers to the finding that when a stimulus from a list is remembered, memory for other stimuli nearby in the list is enhanced

span.label: jump back in time
span.quote: However, unlike short-term memory models, in retrieved temporal context models, the contiguity effect is a result of a “jump back in time.” A repeated stimulus need not cause the same input as it did when it was first presented; a repeated stimulus can recover the state of context that was available before it was initially presented. The recovered state is, in turn, a mixture of the inputs caused by earlier stimuli weighted by their temporal proximity.

span.label: temporal autocorrelation
span.quote: The distribution of lag one regression coefficients across units was significantly greater than zero, mean .094 ± .01, t(269) = 9.31, p < .001 (see Figure 3a ). We refer to units that had a lag one regression coefficient significantly greater than zero (p < .05) as temporally-autocorrelated units. Almost one quarter of all units recorded (.248) were classified as temporally-autocorrelated units.

span.label: ensemble similarity
span.quote: Because of the variability in the number of units across recording sessions ( Table 1 ), we do not simply report means averaged across sessions. Rather, the mean values report the average across units. That is, for the purposes of doing statistics, each unit was treated as a one-cell ensemble. Because recording sessions from a particular patient were separated by at least 48 hours, we treated each unit as an independent observation.

span.label: stimulus repetition (first vs. second presentation) in continuous recognition
span.term: stimulus repetition (first vs. second presentation) in continuous recognition
span.quote: Patients were shown pictures of unknown faces and places, each stimulus repeated once, and asked to indicate whether or not the picture had been previously presented

span.label: stimulus category (faces vs. places), blocked
span.quote: Pictures were shown in four alternating blocks of 20 non-famous faces taken from the Stirling database 1 and 20 unfamiliar indoor and outdoor places.

span.label: lag between an earlier event and the original presentation of the repeated stimulus
span.term: lag between an earlier event and the original presentation of the repeated stimulus
span.quote: For each repeated stimulus, we compared the ensemble activity for that event to preceding events from the same block and aggregated the results, not as a function of the recency of the comparison, but as a function of the lag between the earlier event and the initial presentation of the repeated stimulus.

span.label: average unit firing rate in the 3 s after each stimulus event

span.label: ensemble similarity between event vectors
span.quote: To compare ensemble similarities of event vectors, we z-transformed each unit’s activity across events prior to taking a weighted inner product.
